narrative:
Based on the assessment, the model estimates an 11% chance that you will fail your final year. While this may seem like a small number, it sits just above the 10% threshold that triggers the requirement for remedial courses. This decision exists to give you the best possible chance of success before any difficulties become harder to address.

Looking at what shaped this prediction, three factors stood out most prominently — and importantly, all three actually worked in your favour, pushing the likelihood of failing downward rather than upward.

The most influential factor was your clean academic record: you have no history of past failures, which strongly signals your ability to meet course demands. This was the single strongest indicator in your favour. Second, your ambition to pursue higher education also reduced your predicted risk — every student in a comparable group shares this goal, and that motivation matters. Third, your reason for choosing this school — proximity to home — had a modest positive effect as well, suggesting a practical, stable approach to your education.

So why are you still required to take remedial courses? Because even though these factors reduced your risk, they were not enough to bring the overall prediction below the 10% threshold. Other aspects of your profile — such as your 16 absences, compared to an average of fewer than 3 among students not in this situation — likely contributed to the remaining risk, even if they did not rank among the top three influences.

You should treat the remedial courses as a genuine opportunity. Addressing your attendance in particular could make a meaningful difference going forward.
